summary: A short 1969 note objecting to very high link numbers in the host-host protocol. The author says their site will build its tables around a smaller limit, and that 64 would certainly be sufficient even if 32 seems more realistic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 25 proposes using link numbers no higher than 63 because the author considers 256 numbers more than needed. It also leaves open the view that 32 may be more realistic, while 64 is sufficient.

subtitle: A proposal to keep link numbers at or below 63.

tldr.problem: The protocol had 256 link numbers, more than the author thought were needed, and higher numbers might be useful for instrumentation.
tldr.mechanism: The note suggests that no link number over 63 be used, while noting that 32 may be more realistic and 64 is sufficient.
tldr.outcome: UCLA says it will build its tables to take advantage of the proposed limit; the note does not report wider adoption.

facts.label: Number the author says is sufficient

today: The unit metadata records RFC 25 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The note presents a link-number recommendation and UCLA's plan to use it.

sections.title: Why Use Fewer Link Numbers
sections.content:
The note says 256 link numbers are many more than needed. It also says it may be desirable to reserve one or more numbers for instrumentation.

On these grounds, the author suggests that no link number over 63 be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The author thinks the protocol allows more link numbers than are needed. Keeping the highest numbers unused could leave some available for instrumentation.

sections.title: Proposed Limit and UCLA's Plan
sections.content:
The proposed rule is that no link number over 63 be used. The note says UCLA will implement its tables to take advantage of this limitation.

It adds that 32 may be a more realistic number, while 64 is certainly sufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: The note recommends staying at or below link number 63. UCLA says it will design its tables for that limit, though the author thinks 32 may often be enough.

sections.title: Scope of the Note
sections.content: RFC 25 gives a short recommendation and says how UCLA plans to implement its tables. It does not specify a formal allocation procedure or report that every site adopted the proposed limit.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a brief proposal with an implementation intention from UCLA. The note does not describe a network-wide adoption decision.
